_notes: The 30 Pacific USA fungi (DESIGN-identification.md 8.1, S15), in dex order by
growth form:
1-18   mushrooms (cap and stem)
19-24  brackets (shelf and conk)
25-30  other fungi (cup, coral, puffball, jelly, morel)
fungusClass is one of mushroom / bracket / other_fungus and is editorial judgment
(growth form, not taxonomy — DESIGN.md D13). Ecosystem tags are judgment too,
never fetched.
READ THIS BEFORE EDITING A usesNote.
Dr. Duke's is an ethnobotanical database and has no fungal taxa. There is no
medicinal join for fungi, no medicinalActivities, and — the part that matters —
no Poison record. The rule that makes the PLANT cautions source-driven (a Duke's
Poison record forces a 'Caution:' sentence or the build fails) cannot fire here.
So every caution in this file is one person's sentence, checked by nothing. The
build enforces only what a machine can:
- a fungus carries uses: [] unconditionally, and any row or override trying to
set a use, an edible flag or a Duke's field fails the build (M35);
- EVERY fungus must carry a 'Caution:' sentence, harmless ones included, so the
absence of a warning can never be read as reassurance;
- the note must be that sentence and nothing else — a fungus has no use for the
rest of a note to describe, and the app would drop it on import;
- no text on a fungal record — the note, the description or the habitat prose —
may use an edibility word. Sentences the Wikipedia fetch supplies that do are
dropped before the asset is written.
WHAT A CAUTION SAYS. What the species does to a person, and what it is mistaken
for, drawn from the Wikipedia toxicity / similar-species / identification text the
pipeline collects into cache/fungi_caution_review.txt. It never says a mushroom is
edible, safe, choice or good eating — not even for a chanterelle. The app makes no
edibility claim about a fungus, by design; a person deciding whether to eat one is
not being served by a phone game, and the four deadly species below are in the
list precisely because they are what a beginner's mistake looks like.
'wikipediaTitle' pins the article; 'overrides' pins any output field except the
use fields, which are refused.

species.usesNote: Caution: the western jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus olivascens) is its main look-alike here — true blade-like gills instead of blunt ridges, growing on wood, glowing faintly in the dark — and it causes severe cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea.

Caution: the devil's bolete (Rubroboletus satanas) has a similar shape with a red stem that stains blue, and the very bitter Tylopilus felleus is a frequent confusion; both are told apart only by close examination of the stalk.

Caution: poisonous. It contains ibotenic acid and muscimol; poisonings occur in children and in people who eat it for its psychoactive effects, and it has been confused with red-capped Amanita species elsewhere in the Americas.

Caution: deadly. It carries the amatoxins of the death cap, and of those poisoned by it 40% died. It fruits in spring under oaks and, before the cap opens, has been taken for a meadow mushroom or a puffball.
Caution: deadly, and responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. Half a cap can kill an adult, symptoms begin only 6 to 12 hours later, and the toxins destroy the liver and the kidneys.

Caution: poisonous, more so than the fly agaric. It causes vomiting, diarrhoea and heavy sweating that can bring on severe dehydration, and unlike the blusher (Amanita rubescens) its damaged flesh never turns pink.

Caution: Chlorophyllum molybdites, which causes more poisonings than any other mushroom in America, is confused with it, as are the magpie inkcap and the common inkcap — the latter poisons anyone who has drunk alcohol.

Caution: deadly. This small brown mushroom on rotting conifer wood carries the same amatoxins as the death cap, and has been mistaken for honey mushrooms, for Kuehneromyces mutabilis and for Psilocybe cyanescens.

Caution: poisonous — not lethal, but it causes very severe cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea. It is the chanterelle's look-alike: true blade-like gills rather than ridges, growing straight on wood, and faintly bioluminescent.

Caution: poisonous. Symptoms are delayed 5 to 10 hours and include vomiting, diarrhoea and impaired vision; one autopsied death showed liver failure. The similar Hypholoma capnoides lacks its greenish-yellow gills.

Caution: the deadly Galerina marginata fruits on the same rotting wood and has been mistaken for it. Specimens growing on buckeye or hemlock cause stomach upset, and it disagrees with some people and not others.

Caution: in grass its buttons are confused with the destroying angels (Amanita virosa and kin), which have killed people who took them for this species; an Amanita has a volva at the stem base and gills that stay white.

Caution: poisonous — about half of all Agaricus poisonings are this species, which brings on sweating, flushing and severe stomach cramps. Its stem base stains bright chrome yellow when cut and it smells of ink or phenol.

Caution: the toxic Clitocybe dealbata and C. rivulosa share its lawn rings, and several other small brown mushrooms differ from it only under a microscope. Lawn fungi also take up whatever is sprayed on the grass.

Caution: the deadly Galerina marginata occurs in the same habitat and is one of the small brown mushrooms this is mistaken for; Lactarius species are told from them by a brittle stem that snaps rather than bends.

Caution: serious poisonings have come from confusing it with the poisonous white Amanita smithiana, which grows in the same conifer duff; Russula brevipes and several other pale Tricholoma species also resemble it.

Caution: several small funnel-shaped relatives (Craterellus lutescens, C. odoratus) are separated from it by colour alone, and it fruits on moss and rotten wood where deadly small brown mushrooms also grow.

Caution: the acrid Russula cascadensis and R. vesicatoria look the same and are separated by taste and spore size, and Hygrophorus subalpinus is another look-alike. Acrid Russula species cause vomiting.

Caution: too tough to be food, and a row of look-alikes — false turkey tail (Stereum ostrea), Trametes hirsuta, Bjerkandera adusta and others — are told apart only by the underside, which here is finely pored.

Caution: a woody perennial bracket, indigestible raw and too tough to be food. Ganoderma brownii, G. oregonense and the red-belted conk all resemble it; its white pore surface bruises brown, which is what it is drawn on.

Caution: inedible — a hard woody bracket rather than soft flesh. Ganoderma lucidum, Laricifomes officinalis and Heterobasidion annosum are similar, and all of them mean the conifer carrying them is rotting inside.

Caution: Laetiporus brackets cause swollen lips, nausea and vomiting in some people and not others, and this conifer-growing species is the one most often reported. It is a pathogen of fir, spruce and hemlock, whose wood it rots.
Caution: angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens) shelves on the same conifer wood and was implicated in 17 deaths in Japan in 2004. Some Clitocybe species are poisonous and can resemble a pale oyster.

Caution: implicated in outbreaks of fatal encephalopathy in Japan in 2004 — 59 people fell ill and 17 died, most of them with existing kidney or liver disease. It is thin, white and shelving on conifer wood, like an oyster.

Caution: false morels (Gyromitra species) fruit in the same season and contain gyromitrin, recognised as potentially deadly. A true morel is hollow from cap to stem base and pitted; a false one is folded and brain-like.

Caution: potentially deadly. Its gyromitrin content varies so widely that some people are severely poisoned or die while others eating the same dish show nothing at all, and it is taken for a true morel.

Caution: it is a mould that has overgrown another mushroom, and once the orange crust covers the host that host can no longer be identified; white, pink and yellow moulds of the same kind can be toxic.

Caution: Tremella aurantia is frequently confused with it — thicker lobes, a matte rather than greasy surface, and its host Stereum hirsutum on the same log. Yellow jelly fungi are hard to separate without the host.
Caution: a young destroying angel cut in half is also plain white inside, which is the standard confusion with a puffball; and a puffball whose flesh has begun to yellow or green is breaking down.
Caution: species of Otidea and Caloscypha, some poisonous and some of unknown effect, are confused with it, and the brittle cups are usually broken before they can be examined closely.
